name: Aristarchus
title: Paul's faithful coworker from Thessalonica
summary: Aristarchus from Thessalonica in Macedonia distinguished himself as one of the most steadfast companions in the apostle Paul's missionary work. He was present during the dramatic riot in Ephesus, where he was seized by the crowd along with Gaius, yet he continued to follow Paul on his further journeys through Macedonia, Greece, and all the way to Rome. When Paul was imprisoned in Rome, Aristarchus stood by his side as a fellow prisoner—a designation that underscores his willingness to personally bear the costs of faithfulness to the gospel. His repeated mention in both Acts, Colossians, and Philemon testifies to a man who was deeply trusted within the network of the early church and indispensable in Paul's service.

keyEvents.title: The Riot in Ephesus
keyEvents.description: During the riot led by the silversmith Demetrius in Ephesus, Aristarchus and Gaius, both Macedonians, were dragged into the theater by the angry mob. The incident illustrates the concrete dangers faced by early Christian missionaries.

keyEvents.title: Journey with Paul through Macedonia and Greece
keyEvents.description: Aristarchus from Thessalonica was among those who accompanied Paul on his journey from Ephesus through Macedonia and Greece, and he was one of the companions waiting for the apostle in Troas.

keyEvents.title: The Sea Voyage to Rome
keyEvents.description: When Paul was taken as a prisoner from Caesarea to Rome, Aristarchus from Thessalonica was on board. His presence on this dangerous journey testifies to deep personal loyalty toward the apostle.

keyEvents.title: Fellow Prisoner in Rome
keyEvents.description: In the letter to the Colossians, Paul sends greetings from Aristarchus and refers to him as his fellow prisoner. This suggests that Aristarchus shared Paul's imprisonment in Rome and bore the burden of captivity together with him.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned as a Fellow Worker in the Letter to Philemon
keyEvents.description: Paul mentions Aristarchus among his fellow workers in the greetings of the letter to Philemon, confirming his continued service at the apostle's side.

versions.summary: Aristarchus was a Macedonian Christian from Thessalonica who served as a faithful travel companion and co-worker of the apostle Paul. He was caught up in the riot in Ephesus, traveled with Paul to Jerusalem, and later accompanied him to Rome as a fellow prisoner. He is mentioned as a valuable co-worker in several of Paul's letters.
versions.title: Paul's Faithful Co-Worker
versions.reason: [major] The roles are incomplete. Aristarchus was more than just a 'disciple'. He is explicitly described as a 'fellow worker' (synergos) in Philemon 24, and as a 'fellow prisoner' (synaichmalotos) in Colossians 4:10. These roles should be added to provide a more complete picture.; [minor] The title is good and descriptive, but could also include his origin from Thessalonica to make it more precise.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Notes should be added about the Greek name Aristarchus, the historical context regarding the theater in Ephesus, and the theological significance of the term 'fellow prisoner'.; [minor] The description of the riot in Ephesus could be expanded with additional verses to provide better context, for example Acts 19:28-41 which covers the entire event.

He was caught up in the riot in Ephesus, traveled with Paul to Jerusalem, and later accompanied him to Rome as a fellow prisoner. footnotes.text: The name Aristarchus (Greek: Ἀρίσταρχος, Aristarchos) means 'the best ruler' or 'the foremost leader', composed of the Greek words 'aristos' (best) and 'archein' (to rule/lead). It was a common Greek name in the Hellenistic world.

The theater in Ephesus, where Aristarchus was dragged into during the riot, is one of the best-preserved ancient theaters in the world. It could hold approximately 25,000 spectators and was used for both entertainment and public assemblies. Archaeological excavations have confirmed its existence and size.

The term 'fellow prisoner' (Greek: synaichmalōtos) that Paul uses regarding Aristarchus in Colossians 4:10 is debated among scholars. Some argue it should be understood literally, meaning Aristarchus shared Paul's physical imprisonment. Others interpret it metaphorically as a spiritual designation for someone who is a 'prisoner of war' in Christ's service. The literal interpretation is supported by the fact that Aristarchus actually traveled with Paul to Rome.

Thessalonica (today's Thessaloniki) was the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia and an important trading city along the Via Egnatia. The city had a significant Jewish population and a synagogue (Acts 17:1). That Aristarchus came from there shows that the early church in Thessalonica nurtured dedicated workers for the further Christian mission.

In early church tradition, some sources count Aristarchus among the seventy disciples whom Jesus sent out (Luke 10:1). According to later traditions, he became bishop of Apamea in Syria, and certain martyrologies claim he suffered martyrdom during Nero's persecutions, but these traditions have uncertain historical grounding.

Macedonia was an important Roman province in the first century, and Macedonian Christians played a prominent role in the early church's missionary work. Besides Aristarchus, other Macedonians such as Gaius, Secundus, and Sopater are mentioned among Paul's traveling companions (Acts 20:4), indicating that the Macedonian churches were particularly active in supporting Paul's ministry.
